posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Congratulations, Danny. I'm thinking of buying a laser like yours, and I was wondering if you could share some information about it. It seems that these lasers appear on eBay once in a while, often in need of repair. The purchase price should be within the means of many holographers. I guess the repair work (i.e., diode replacement) is the expensive part, but at least someone could pay for the whole thing in two parts (the initial purchase, then the repair). Can you share what the repair cost was, and the approximate amount of time it took?

I looked at the specifications at:

[http://lasers.mellesgriot.com/Specsheet.asp?CatID=11421](http://lasers.mellesgriot.com/Specsheet.asp?CatID=11421)

Is yours the 85 BLD 605? (The two-beam model with 200mW for each beam) I assume that both beams come from the same cavity, and I'm guessing that they are mutually coherent (one useable for the reference beam, and the other for the object). I see the beams are somewhat elliptical (0.15mm X 0.29mm) and I'm wondering if this would complicate the use of a spatial filter. (They have other, lower-power models that have a circular beam shape).

They way I see it now, the Melles-Griot lasers are the best solution for use in color holography. Substantial power is needed in the appropriate region of the blue spectrum (with enough coherence), and all of these requirements are met. In comparison to an argon laser, there's no need for three-phase power or water cooling (involving the additional expense of a chiller, unless the water goes straight down the drain, which can get expensive for people with municipal water). From what I hear, the electrical consumption of ion lasers is quite high also.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
I believe this statement, "Each beam is linearly polarized and can be treated optically as emanating from two waists located in the cavity" indicates the two beams act as if they are from two different cavities thus they would not be able to be used as Reference and Object beams to one another. I think that is why the separate the two beams.

Anyone else know for sure what "emanating from two waists" means?

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: I believe it's from the same cavity but the cavity geometry is such that it has two "chambers" or "waists". I imagine the cavity geometry as an "H" with the long arms being the lasing media.
